title: Molecular Insights into Gas Nanofilms Confined Between Bulk Liquid Phases
authors: Yafan Yang, Zufeng Zuo, Xingyu Zhao, Shuyu Sun, Denvid Lau
abstract: Nanometer-thick fluid films play a critical role in confined multiphase processes, yet the thermodynamics and stability of free gas nanofilms remain poorly understood compared with their liquid counterparts. Here, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are employed to systematically investigate gas nanofilms confined between bulk liquid phases using Lennard-Jones argon as a model system. The results show that the surface tension decreases exponentially with decreasing film thickness, accompanied by an increasing magnitude of the negative disjoining pressure. Upon thinning, the planar gas film undergoes a distinct morphological transition from a stable planar state to a transient or persistent spherical bubble through the formation and growth of a liquid bridge. The film surface area strongly affects its thermodynamic properties, with larger areas producing stronger thickness dependence and larger deviations from classical density functional theory (cDFT) predictions. The closer agreement between MD and cDFT at smaller surface areas suggests that the discrepancy primarily arises from thermal capillary-wave fluctuations, which are included in MD but omitted in mean-field cDFT. Moreover, at small film thicknesses, the magnitude of the disjoining pressure increases with decreasing temperature, consistent with the enhanced sensitivity of the confined gas phase to thickness variations and contrasting with the trend generally reported for liquid nanofilms. These findings provide molecular insights into the thermodynamics and stability of gas nanofilms, with implications for confined multiphase transport and droplet coalescence.
summary: This work uses molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the thermodynamics and stability of gas nanofilms confined by liquid phases. Key findings include the exponential decrease of surface tension and a morphological transition to spherical bubbles upon thinning. The research highlights the importance of thermal fluctuations in accurately modeling these nanoscale interfacial phenomena.
main_problem: The study aims to understand the poorly understood thermodynamics and stability of free gas nanofilms confined between bulk liquid phases.
main_result: The surface tension decreases exponentially with film thickness, and the film undergoes a morphological transition from planar to spherical bubble upon thinning. The discrepancy between MD and cDFT is attributed to thermal capillary-wave fluctuations.
method: Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations are employed alongside a Gibbs surface thermodynamic framework to derive relationships between surface tension and disjoining pressure.
model_or_system: The system modeled is a gas nanofilm confined between two bulk liquid phases, using Lennard-Jones argon as a representative model system.
key_observables: Surface tension ($\sigma_f$), disjoining pressure ($\Pi$), film thickness ($h$), and gas-phase morphology.
important_parameters: Film thickness ($h$), temperature ($T$), and lateral surface area ($A$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Gibbs surface formulation and contrasts the system behavior with established liquid nanofilm models, noting the importance of including thermal fluctuations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dependence of surface tension and disjoining pressure on film thickness and temperature, and show time evolution of gas-phase morphologies (planar to spherical bubble).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the thermodynamic framework, derives key relationships between surface tension and disjoining pressure, uses MD simulations to calculate these properties, and analyzes the resulting morphological transitions and theoretical discrepancies.
why_interesting: The study provides detailed molecular insights into phase transitions and interfacial thermodynamics in confined geometries, which are fundamental concepts in statistical mechanics and many-body physics.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) Schematic illustration of a gas nanofilm (f) confined within a pore. The nanofilm is connected to the bulk gas (g) through a Plateau-border meniscus and is sandwiched between two bulk liquid (l) phases. (b) Mechanical equilibrium of the confined nanofilm, illustrating the disjoining pressure Π, film tension γf, and surface tension σf acting on the film. (c) Molecular dynamics simulation setup employed to determine the film surface tension σf.

Figure 2: Interfacial properties of gas nanofilms at 120 K with a surface area of 49.056× 49.056 ˚A 2: (a) film surface tension, σf, as a function of film thickness, h; (b) disjoining pressure, Π, as a function of film thickness, h; and (c) Π as a function of h−3. Dashed lines represent linear fits. The cDFT results shown in (b) and (c) are reproduced from Ref. [28].

Figure 3: Time evolution of gas-phase morphologies for systems with a surface area of 49.056 × 49.056 ˚A 2 at 120 K and different initial planar film thicknesses. Planar gas films are enclosed by black dotted boxes, while spherical gas bubbles are indicated by black dotted circles.

Figure 4: Interfacial properties of gas nanofilms at 120 K with different surface areas: (a) film surface tension, σf, as a function of film thickness, h; (b) disjoining pressure, Π, as a function of film thickness, h; and (c) Π as a function of h−3. Dashed lines represent linear fits. The cDFT results shown in (b) and (c) are reproduced from Ref. [28].
